title: Testing
blurb: Prove your code works — and keep it working as it grows.

lessons.title: Unit testing
lessons.explain: A unit test checks one small piece of behavior in isolation. Arrange inputs, act (call the function), assert the expected output.
objectives: Write a unit test that isolates and verifies one piece of behavior
Explain how assert changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect assert with arrange-act-assert and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
commonMistakes: Writing a test with no real assertion -- the code runs but nothing is actually verified as correct.
lessons.explanation: A unit test checks one small piece of behavior in isolation. Arrange inputs, act (call the function), assert the expected output.

lessons.title: Integration tests
objectives: Distinguish integration tests from unit tests
Explain how integration test changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect integration test with component boundaries and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: An integration test checks that multiple components work correctly TOGETHER -- a database, an API, and business logic interacting -- unlike a unit test, which isolates one function or class alone. Integration tests catch bugs that only appear at the boundaries between components, but they're typically slower and more complex to set up than unit tests.
examples:
# unit test: does calculate_total() return the right number, in isolation?
# integration test: does the checkout FLOW correctly save an order to the
# real database AND correctly call the payment API AND return a receipt?
commonMistakes: Only writing unit tests and assuming components will work correctly together -- integration bugs specifically happen AT the boundaries unit tests can't see.
lessons.careerRelevance: A healthy test suite needs both unit and integration tests -- they catch different categories of bugs.

lessons.title: Mocking
objectives: Use mocks to isolate a unit test from its real dependencies
Explain how mock changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect mock with mocking and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A mock is a fake stand-in for a real dependency (a database, an external API) used in a unit test, so the test doesn't actually hit the network or a real database -- making it fast, reliable, and independent of the real service being available.
examples:
from unittest.mock import Mock
payment_api = Mock()
payment_api.charge.return_value = {'status': 'success'}

result = process_order(payment_api)
payment_api.charge.assert_called_once()
commonMistakes: Over-mocking so heavily that the test no longer verifies anything meaningful about the real code's behavior.
lessons.careerRelevance: Mocking is essential for fast, reliable unit tests that don't depend on real external services being up.

lessons.title: Test coverage
objectives: Interpret test coverage and its limits
Explain how coverage changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect coverage with test coverage and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Test coverage measures what percentage of your code actually runs during your test suite. High coverage is a useful signal, but it's not the same as correctness -- a line can be 'covered' by a test that runs it without actually checking the output is right.
examples:
# a test that calls a function but asserts nothing meaningful:
def test_process():
    process(data)   # covered! but nothing was actually verified

# a real test:
def test_process():
    result = process(data)
    assert result == expected
commonMistakes: Chasing a high coverage percentage as the goal itself, rather than writing tests that actually verify correct behavior.
lessons.careerRelevance: Coverage is a useful metric to track, but experienced engineers know not to over-trust it alone.

lessons.title: Regression testing
objectives: Explain why regression tests matter as code changes over time
Explain how regression changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect regression with regression test and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A regression is when a previously-working feature breaks due to a later change. A regression test suite -- run before every change ships -- catches this by re-verifying old behavior still holds, not just the new feature being added.
examples:
# every time you fix a bug, add a test for that EXACT bug --
# this becomes a permanent regression test, ensuring it never
# silently comes back in a future change
commonMistakes: Fixing a bug without adding a test for it -- the same bug can silently resurface in a later change with nothing to catch it.
lessons.careerRelevance: A strong regression suite is exactly what lets a real, growing codebase change safely over its lifetime.

lessons.title: Test-Driven Development: an overview
objectives: Describe the TDD cycle: red, green, refactor
Explain how TDD changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect TDD with red green refactor and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Test-Driven Development writes a failing test FIRST (red), then writes the minimum code to make it pass (green), then improves the code's structure without changing its behavior (refactor) -- repeating this cycle for each small piece of functionality.
examples:
# 1. RED: write a test for behavior that doesn't exist yet -- it fails
def test_add():
    assert add(2, 3) == 5   # fails -- add() doesn't exist yet

# 2. GREEN: write just enough code to pass
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

# 3. REFACTOR: clean up if needed, tests still pass
commonMistakes: Writing all the implementation code first and adding tests as an afterthought -- this is the opposite of TDD's intended discipline.
lessons.careerRelevance: TDD is a real, actively-practiced methodology at many companies, even if not used universally.
lessons.explain: Test-Driven Development writes a failing test FIRST (red), then writes the minimum code to make it pass (green), then improves the code's structure without changing its behavior (refactor) -- repeating this cycle for each small piece of functionality.
lessons.example:

# 2. GREEN: write just enough code to pass
def add(a, b): return a + b

# 3. REFACTOR: clean up if needed, tests still pass

lessons.title: Debugging failing tests
objectives: Apply a systematic workflow when a test fails
Explain how fail changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect fail with actual vs expected and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: When a test fails, first check whether the TEST or the CODE is wrong -- a failing test isn't automatically proof of a code bug; the test itself might have a mistaken expectation. Read the actual vs expected output the test reports, and reproduce the failure in isolation before trying a fix.
examples:
# test failure workflow:
# 1. read the actual vs expected values in the failure output
# 2. is the code wrong, or is the test's expectation wrong?
# 3. reproduce in isolation (run just that one test)
# 4. fix, then re-run the FULL suite to check nothing else broke
commonMistakes: Assuming a failing test always means the code is broken, without first checking whether the test's own expectation is actually correct.
lessons.careerRelevance: This systematic workflow prevents wasted time chasing the wrong cause when a test suite reports a failure.

lessons.title: The testing pyramid & strategy
objectives: Balance unit, integration, and end-to-end tests
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: browser end-to-end automation (Playwright/Selenium).
Explain how testing pyramid changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect testing pyramid with end-to-end test and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: The testing pyramid suggests having MANY fast unit tests, FEWER integration tests, and VERY FEW slow, expensive end-to-end tests (which drive the whole system through its real UI/API).
examples:
# testing pyramid shape (bottom to top):
# many unit tests (fast, cheap, isolated)
# fewer integration tests (slower, test real components together)
# very few end-to-end tests (slowest, test the whole system like a real user)
commonMistakes: Building an 'inverted pyramid' -- mostly slow end-to-end tests and few unit tests -- which makes the whole suite slow and fragile.
lessons.careerRelevance: Testing strategy and the pyramid shape are common real architecture and code-review discussion points. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: Writing clear tests & assertions
objectives: Write test names and assertions that are genuinely useful when they fail
Explain how test naming changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect test naming with clear assertions and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A good test name describes the SPECIFIC behavior being verified (test_returns_error_for_negative_input), not a vague name like test1. A good assertion checks the actual expected outcome specifically, so when it fails, the failure message tells you exactly what went wrong without needing to dig through the test's internals.
commonMistakes: Writing vague test names and assertions that don't clearly state what's actually being verified, making failures hard to diagnose later.
lessons.careerRelevance: Clear, well-named tests double as living documentation of what the code is actually supposed to do.

lessons.title: TDD in practice: Red → Green → Refactor
objectives: Apply TDD to business logic by writing a failing behavior test before implementation
Explain how Red-Green-Refactor changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Red-Green-Refactor with edge cases and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explain: Test-driven development is a short feedback loop: write one small test that fails for the right reason, implement the simplest behavior that makes it pass, then refactor while keeping all tests green. Good TDD tests describe observable behavior rather than private implementation details.
lessons.example: Example sequence for transfer(): 1) test a normal transfer; 2) make it pass; 3) test insufficient funds; 4) make it pass; 5) test same-account or invalid amount; 6) refactor shared validation while every test remains green.
commonMistakes: Writing the entire implementation first and then calling the later test suite TDD.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in modern software/backend internship requirements or technical interviews and strengthens transferable engineering fundamentals.

lessons.title: Testing concurrent & transactional behavior
objectives: Design tests for race conditions, transaction boundaries, retries, and invariants
Explain how concurrency test changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect concurrency test with invariant and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explain: Concurrency tests should check invariants rather than depend on lucky timing. For a money-transfer service, useful invariants include total money remaining constant, no negative balance when forbidden, and a failed transaction leaving both accounts unchanged.
lessons.example: Instead of sleep-based tests, coordinate two workers so both reach a known point before releasing them. After both finish, assert the invariant on final balances and verify that retries do not double-apply the transfer.
commonMistakes: Using arbitrary sleep() calls and assuming a race happened.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in modern software/backend internship requirements or technical interviews and strengthens transferable engineering fundamentals.

description: Prove your code works — and keep it working as it grows.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the difference between a unit test and an integration test, and when do you need both?
interviewPreparation.a: A unit test isolates one function or component, typically mocking its dependencies; an integration test exercises a real boundary between components (e.g. a function actually talking to a real or test database). You need both -- unit tests catch logic errors cheaply and fast, integration tests catch the failures that only show up when real pieces are wired together.

interviewPreparation.q: Why isn't a high coverage percentage the same as a good test suite?
interviewPreparation.a: Coverage only measures whether a line of code executed during tests, not whether anything meaningful was actually asserted about its behavior -- a test that calls a function with no assertions can show 100% coverage on that function while catching zero real bugs. Coverage is a useful signal for what's UNtested, not proof that what IS tested is well-tested.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you decide when to use a mock versus calling the real dependency in a test?
interviewPreparation.a: Mock dependencies that are slow, external, non-deterministic, or costly to call repeatedly (a payment API, an email service, real network calls) so unit tests stay fast and reliable; use the real thing (or a real integration test) when you specifically need to verify the actual integration works, not just your code's logic in isolation.

interviewPreparation.q: A test passes locally but fails in CI. How do you approach debugging that?
interviewPreparation.a: Suspect something the test doesn't fully control: shared state between tests, system time, test execution order, or an environment difference (a clean database in CI vs. leftover local state). Try to reproduce it by running just that test repeatedly and in isolation, rather than assuming it's a CI infrastructure problem before ruling out the test itself.

interviewPreparation.q: How does TDD (red-green-refactor) actually change how you design code, beyond just testing it?
interviewPreparation.a: Writing the failing test first forces you to think about the function's actual interface and expected behavior before implementation details, which tends to produce more testable, more decoupled code -- it's as much a design discipline as a testing one, which is why some teams use it even when they don't obsess over coverage numbers afterward.

capstone.title: Design and defend a real test strategy, not just a passing test suite
capstone.description: Take a nontrivial function or small module (from a previous course capstone, or new) and build out a genuinely layered test suite: real unit tests, at least one integration test at a real component boundary, deliberate use of mocks where a dependency shouldn't be hit directly, and a written test-strategy justification using the testing pyramid -- not just chasing a coverage percentage. This capstone is about test suite QUALITY and reasoning, the skill that separates 'tests exist' from 'these tests would actually catch a real regression.'
deliverables: A unit test suite covering real edge cases, not just the happy path (built test-first via TDD for at least one function)
At least one integration test exercising a real component boundary (e.g. a function plus the database or API it calls)
At least one deliberate mock, with a written justification for why that dependency shouldn't be hit directly in this test
A coverage report plus a written note on one thing coverage percentage alone doesn't tell you (tying back to what 'meaningless coverage' actually means)
A short written test strategy citing the testing pyramid: what you tested at which layer, and why
capstone.portfolioTips: The written test-strategy justification is the differentiator here -- a reviewer skimming a repo full of green tests can't tell if you understand WHY the suite is shaped that way; a short, clear rationale proves you do.

industryUsage.usage: Popularized the testing pyramid concept broadly in the industry, and is well known for treating test suite quality and coverage discipline as a core engineering practice, not an afterthought.
Invests heavily in automated regression testing to support extremely frequent deployments, since a large, reliable test suite is what makes shipping many times a day survivable.
As a fintech shipping frequent changes to financial logic, treats meaningful test coverage (not just a percentage) as a real safety requirement, not a formality.
